Case Study 01

Under Control

A narrative decision game where you play the newly appointed CEO of a fashion conglomerate, days after a federal indictment exposes the company's supply chain. Every choice trades off profit, risk, public trust, and morale — and the scenarios are built on real reporting about labor and environmental practices in fast fashion.

ROLE
UI/UX design + research
TEAM
Collaborative, class project
TOOL
Figma (click-through prototype)
TIMELINE
7-day narrative arc

The premise

Under Control puts the player in the seat of "Evan," installed as CEO of Loom Industries after the previous CEO is indicted for fraud, environmental crimes, and conspiracy. The game runs over a 7-day arc. Each day the player has to weigh decisions — press interviews, supplier contracts, worker treatment — against four visible metrics: profit, risk, public trust, and morale.

My role was UI/UX design and research. The research half mattered as much as the interface half: the scenarios aren't invented. Day 2's news-article sequence, for example, cites real reporting — a case where thousands of garment workers were denied owed wages, and separately, industry findings on Shein's emissions and labor conditions. The interface had to make that research land inside a game loop, not just sit next to it.

Designing the dashboard as the throughline

The hardest UI problem was the "Executive Dashboard" — the screen the player returns to constantly. It needed to hold a lot at once: which day you're on, an in-fiction messaging/notification system (email, phone, alerts), and the four-metric tracker (profit, risk, public trust, morale) without turning into a cluttered stat sheet.

I leaned on a real corporate-software visual language on purpose — left icon rail, top identity block ("Good morning, Evan"), right-aligned metric bars — because the whole premise is that you're inhabiting a role built out of dashboards and detachment. The UI's coldness is doing narrative work, not just organizing information.

Bringing tension into secondary screens

Two screens I'm most happy with are ones that could easily have been afterthoughts: the meeting queue and the phone call interstitial.

  • 01Waiting room / waitlist. Journalists queue by urgency (high/medium/low), and the player has to actively triage — "see now" versus "send to room" — inside a literal waiting-room illustration. The environment art (a moody red lounge) does the atmosphere work so the UI card on top can stay purely functional.
  • 02Incoming call screen. Styled like a real phone call UI — mute, speaker, end call — deliberately breaking from the dashboard's visual language. It's a small moment of screen-native realism amid all the diegetic corporate chrome, which makes the "you are being paged constantly" pressure of the role feel more physical.

What I'd do differently

The prototype is click-through only — there's no underlying state engine, so the metric bars are illustrative rather than actually reactive to player choices yet. If I extended this, the priority would be wiring the four metrics to real branching logic (in Figma via variables/conditional logic, or porting the flow to Twine/Ren'Py) so a bad press day visibly drags down public trust in the next scene, instead of the dashboard being a static mockup of state.

I'd also want to pressure-test the icon rail against someone unfamiliar with the game — right now it assumes the player already knows what each icon (mail, phone, alert, grid) does contextually.

Case Study 02

Carbon Choice

A daily-decision sustainability game built for INFO 498. The player picks a character archetype, then works through a day of small choices — commute, meals, purchases — while three competing meters move in response: carbon footprint, happiness, and budget. An AI companion, EVA, narrates and nudges throughout.

ROLE
UI/UX design
TEAM
4-person team, INFO 498
BUILD
HTML/CSS + Ren'Py scripts
STATUS
Playable demo, GitHub Pages

The core problem: three meters, one screen

Most "choices matter" games track a single resource. Carbon Choice tracks three at once — carbon footprint, happiness, and budget — and they don't move together. The cheapest option is sometimes the most carbon-heavy. The happiest option sometimes blows the budget. The UI's job was to make that tension visible at a glance, every single decision, without turning the screen into a spreadsheet.

Carbon20kg
Happiness7 / 10
Budget$60

Keeping all three legible at once meant giving each one a distinct icon and unit rather than normalizing them into identical bars — a kg figure reads differently than a dollar figure, and that difference is the point of the game.

Character select as a design lever, not just flavor

Before the daily loop starts, the player picks a character — and the choice isn't cosmetic. Each archetype starts the day with a different constraint, which changes what "a good decision" even looks like.

Student
Low budget, high happiness reset
Parent
Time stress, family focus
Worker
Higher budget, higher carbon
Eco Influencer
Unlocks after earning "Eco Champion"

The locked fourth character (unlocked by reaching "Eco Champion" status) was a deliberate retention hook — it gives a reason to replay with a harder, more specialized build once you understand the base systems.

EVA: a UI element that's also a character

EVA is the game's AI companion, and functionally, EVA is also a UI pattern — a persistent coaching/feedback layer that appears at decision points instead of a generic tooltip or tutorial popup.

EVA
"Let's see how today goes! Remember, every small choice adds up. I'll be here to guide you along the way."

Routing feedback through a character voice rather than a system message kept the tone encouraging instead of punitive — important for a game whose entire subject is "you will sometimes make the carbon-heavy choice, and that's fine, here's what it cost."

The loop, end to end

  1. Player picks a character archetype, setting their starting constraints.
  2. EVA introduces the day's challenge and the decision count ("Decision 1 of 6").
  3. Each decision updates carbon, happiness, and budget simultaneously — no isolated single-stat choices.
  4. An end-of-day summary totals all three meters, then offers Play Again or Main Menu.

What I'd do differently

The current build is a strong systems demo but a visually plain one — the HTML/CSS implementation prioritized getting the three-meter logic working over a distinctive visual identity. If I revisited this, I'd bring the same "make the tradeoff visible at a glance" thinking into a more considered layout: maybe a literal balance/scale metaphor for the three meters instead of stacked rows, so the tension between them is spatial, not just numeric.
